h1:
Ta Phraya National Park
Quiet Forest, Ridge Views and Khmer Stone Cuts
intro: Ta Phraya is a stretch of forest in eastern Sa Kaeo that stays quiet and sees far fewer visitors than Pang Sida, mostly because it sits deep out toward Ta Phraya district on the Cambodian border. The park runs along the Banthat–Phanom Dong Rak range, which acts like a natural wall between Thailand and Cambodia. What most people come for are the ridge-top viewpoints that look across into Cambodian territory, the sunrise spots, and the "stone quarry" where sandstone was cut to build Khmer temples a thousand years ago. We've pulled together what you can actually do here in 2026, including entry fees, where to stay, how to get there, and what to watch out for near the border.

blocks.html: Ta Phraya National Park covers roughly 594 square kilometres across two provinces, Sa Kaeo and Buriram. It stretches in a long band along the Banthat range, part of the Phanom Dong Rak mountains that form the Thailand–Cambodia border. The draw here isn't big waterfalls but the atmosphere: a quiet forest, ridge-top viewpoints that look down on the Cambodian plains below, a night sky dark enough to show the stars clearly, and traces of Khmer history embedded in the rock. The park headquarters sits around Thap Rat sub-district in Ta Phraya district, a fair distance from Sa Kaeo town. It suits travellers who want to get away from the noise and spend time in a real forest.

blocks.text: Banthat Range and Pha Daeng Viewpoints

blocks.html: The main reason people make the trip to Ta Phraya is the ridge-top viewpoints. The well-known ones are the Banthat Range viewpoint and Pha Daeng viewpoint, a high cliff that looks out over a wide swathe of forest and the Cambodian plains stretching as far as you can see. In the early morning you'll often find a sea of mist hanging in the valleys, and people who stay overnight tend to get up early and walk up to wait for the sunrise. Park rangers usually have you start walking around 4:30 a.m. to catch the first light, since it's a fair hike up from the accommodation area. The trail is forest and rock, so bring a torch and shoes with good grip.

items: Banthat Range viewpoint — looks across the ridge to the Cambodian plains, the most popular spot for sunrise
Pha Daeng viewpoint — a high cliff with a wide forest view, great for photos in the misty morning and the warm light of late afternoon
For sunrise — you need to set off around 04:30, bring a torch and allow time for the climb
Cool season — November to February brings cool air, clear skies and the best odds of a sea of mist

blocks.title: Getting ready for the viewpoint climb
blocks.html: The walk up to the viewpoint is on foot through dark forest before dawn, so bring a torch or headlamp. In the cool season wear a warm layer, because the ridge is windy and much colder than down below. Let a ranger know before you head up and don't wander off the trail, because this area sits right against the border. Stick only to the routes the park marks out.

blocks.text: The Stone Quarry — Khmer Temple Cut Marks

blocks.html: Another thing that sets Ta Phraya apart from other forests is the "stone quarry," a large expanse of sandstone that still shows clear marks where blocks were cut in neat squares. Archaeologists believe this was a sandstone source during the height of Khmer power, used to build temples and carve Buddha images at the religious sites around here. The sandstone here is fine-grained with a pale green tinge, and as you walk across the slab you'll see saw lines, chisel marks and blocks that were cut but never moved, as if you've stepped back onto a craftsman's worksite from a thousand years ago. It's the spot that ties the Ta Phraya forest to the traces of Khmer civilisation scattered across Sa Kaeo.

The stone quarry is within the park but you reach it on foot along a nature trail. The distance isn't far, but the path is forest and rock, so ask the rangers about the route and the hours it's open, because some areas near the border may have restrictions at times. If you come in the rainy season the rock surface can be slippery, so take extra care.

blocks.text: Dark-Sky Reserve — Stargazing in the Forest

blocks.html: Because Ta Phraya is far from any town and there's almost no light pollution, it has been designated one of Thailand's Dark Sky reserves. On clear nights, especially in the cool season, the sky fills with stars, and on some nights you can make out the band of the Milky Way with the naked eye. People who camp overnight often stay up to stargaze after watching the sunset, an activity that costs nothing beyond lying back and looking up. If you're set on photographing the stars, check for the dark-moon window, when there's little moonlight and the stars show up the clearest.

blocks.title: Getting good star photos
blocks.html: Pick a dark-moon night in the cool season when the sky is clear. Carry a red-light torch to get around so you don't ruin other people's night vision while they're stargazing. Bring a warm layer and a blanket, because it gets very cold on the ridge late at night. If you're shooting stars, take a tripod, and check the forecast first, because if the sky clouds over you won't see a thing.

blocks.text: Quiet Forest and Nature Around the Park

blocks.html: Ta Phraya's charm is its quiet. The forest here is dry dipterocarp mixed with dry evergreen along the slopes, with nature trails for walking and watching the plants and forest birds. Along the way you might spot birds, squirrels, and signs of larger animals deeper in the forest, and because fewer people come here than to the more popular parks, the atmosphere is genuinely natural and uncrowded. If you like peace and quiet and want to be in the forest without any noise, you'll like it here. If you're after big waterfalls or lots of activities, Pang Sida may suit you better.

items: Park entry fee — around 20 THB per adult for Thais, 10 THB for children, about 30 THB per car and 20 THB for motorcycles
Camping ground — there's a ground for pitching tents year-round, but you need to bring your own tent, bedding and food; facilities are limited
Park bungalows — the park has bungalows you can book in advance through the National Parks online booking system (nps.dnp.go.th)
Stock up on supplies — there's no shop or large restaurant inside the park like the popular ones have, so buy water and food in Ta Phraya town first

blocks.title: Call ahead before you go
blocks.html: Ta Phraya doesn't get many visitors and its online information is slow to update, so before you travel it's worth calling the park headquarters (the government line 0 3724 7933 or the Ta Phraya National Park Facebook page) about which routes are open, road conditions and booking lodging, because some routes near the border may close from time to time depending on the situation.

The park headquarters sits around Thap Rat sub-district in Ta Phraya district, the easternmost district of Sa Kaeo, right on the border. The most convenient way is to drive yourself. From Sa Kaeo town take Highway 348 (Sa Kaeo–Ta Phraya–Buriram) toward Ta Phraya district, then turn onto the side road to the park following the signs. The final stretch is an uphill mountain road; a sedan can manage it but drive carefully, especially in the rainy season. Sa Kaeo has no airport and no public transport running directly to the park, so without your own vehicle you'll need to rent a car or hire one from town.

Because Ta Phraya sits right against the Thailand–Cambodia border, you need to check carefully about access and border crossing before you go. The border situation around here can change from time to time, and some routes or viewpoints may close temporarily for security reasons. The park is not a border crossing point, so do not walk across the boundary into Cambodia under any circumstances. Stay on the routes the rangers mark out, and always check the area's open status with the park before you set off.

Ta Phraya is most fun if you stay overnight, since the highlights like sunrise and stargazing mean staying through the night. But if you're short on time you can do it as a morning-to-evening day trip focused on the viewpoints and the stone quarry. Here's a rough plan you can actually follow, adjustable by season (the cool season is best for the sea of mist and stargazing, while in the rainy season the rock is slippery so take care).

blocks.title: Pack before you head into the forest
blocks.html: Get your drinking water, food, insect repellent, torch, warm layer and non-slip shoes ready, because facilities inside the park are limited and phone signal is weak. Pack out all your trash every time, don't feed the wildlife, and most importantly, stay on the marked routes and don't walk near the border on your own.

faq.q: What's worth seeing at Ta Phraya National Park?
faq.a: The highlights are the ridge-top viewpoints like the Banthat Range and Pha Daeng viewpoints, which look across into Cambodia; the sunrise and the cool-season sea of mist; the stone quarry where sandstone was cut to build Khmer temples a thousand years ago; and stargazing in the forest, since this is a dark-sky reserve. It suits people who like a quiet, uncrowded forest.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee at Ta Phraya?
faq.a: Entry for Thai visitors is around 20 THB per adult, 10 THB for children, about 30 THB per car and 20 THB for motorcycles. If you camp, there's a ground open year-round but you need to bring your own tent and bedding. Bungalows are booked in advance through the National Parks website.

faq.q: How does Ta Phraya differ from Pang Sida, and which should I visit?
faq.a: Pang Sida is known for waterfalls and the early-rainy-season butterfly season; it sees more visitors and has better facilities. Ta Phraya is known for its border-ridge viewpoints, stargazing and the Khmer-era stone quarry, with a quieter atmosphere and fewer people. If you want to play in waterfalls, choose Pang Sida; if you want mountain views, stargazing and peace and quiet, choose Ta Phraya.

faq.q: How do I get to Ta Phraya, and can I use public transport?
faq.a: The most convenient way is to drive yourself. From Sa Kaeo town take Highway 348 toward Ta Phraya district, then turn into the park following the signs. Sa Kaeo has no airport and no public transport running directly to the park, so without your own vehicle you'll need to rent a car or hire one from town. It's worth calling the park to check road conditions before you go.

faq.q: Ta Phraya is on the border — is it safe to visit?
faq.a: The park itself is open to visitors as usual, but because it sits along the Banthat range that forms the Thailand–Cambodia border, the border situation can change from time to time and some routes or viewpoints may close temporarily. Always check the area's open status with the park headquarters before travelling, stay on the routes the rangers mark out, and never walk across the boundary into Cambodia under any circumstances.
